Title: Quantum Dynamics via Score Matching on Bohmian Trajectories
Text:
Quantum Dynamics via Score Matching on Bohmian Trajectories
Lei Wang1, ∗
1Beijing National Laboratory for Condensed Matter Physics and Institute of Physics,
Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China
(Dated: April 29, 2026)
We solve the time-dependent Schr¨odinger equation by learning the score function, the gradient of
the log-probability density, on Bohmian trajectories. In Bohm’s formulation of quantum mechan-
ics, particles follow deterministic paths under the classical potential supplemented by a quantum
potential depending on the score function of the evolving density.
These non-crossing Bohmian
trajectories form a continuous normalizing flow governed by the score. We parametrize the score
with a neural network and minimize a self-consistent Fisher divergence between the network and the
score of the resulting density. We prove that the zero-loss minimizer of this self-consistent objective
recovers Schr¨odinger dynamics for nodeless wave functions, a condition naturally met in quantum
vibrations of atoms. We demonstrate the approach on wavepacket splitting in a double-well poten-
tial and anharmonic vibrations of a Morse chain. By recasting real-time quantum dynamics as a
self-consistent score-driven normalizing flow, this framework opens the time-dependent Schr¨odinger
equation to the rapidly advancing toolkit of modern generative modeling.

In Eq. (5) the phase S no longer appears as a dynamical
field: v is propagated directly and Q depends only on the
score s via Eq. (4), so the complex phase need not be rep-
resented along the trajectory [15, 16]. The phase enters
only through the initial condition v(0) = ∇S(x, 0)/m
(trivially zero when the initial wave function is real), and
S can be reconstructed post hoc by integrating Eq. (3)
along trajectories if desired. The practical difficulty, how-
ever, is that integrating Eq. (5) requires the quantum
force −∇Q, which depends on the score s of the evolving
density. This score is itself unknown and must be deter-
mined self-consistently. References [3, 4] pioneered quan-
tum trajectory methods by representing the density on a
moving mesh and propagating the hydrodynamic equa-
tions directly. References [15, 16] eliminated the mesh by
fitting s from the particle ensemble via a polynomial ba-
sis and a functional equivalent to Hyv¨arinen score match-
ing [17]. Ref. [18] used a Bayesian Gaussian mixture for
the same purpose. These methods fit the score pointwise
at each timestep using a limited basis (polynomials or
Gaussian mixtures), without a global variational princi-
ple connecting successive times.
In this Letter, we instead parametrize the score with a
neural network sθ(x, t) and train it end-to-end by min-
imizing a single Fisher-divergence objective, simultane-
ously lifting the basis-set restriction and enforcing space-
time self-consistency. The resulting quantum potential
drives a continuous normalizing flow from the initial den-
sity, and any zero-loss minimizer of the objective recovers
the Schr¨odinger solution.
Theory—
The central idea is to train the score net-
work by minimizing the mismatch between sθ and the
score of its own implied density. The training objective
is the Fisher divergence:

Since L ≥0 with equality iff sθ = ∇ln ρθ, minimizing L
drives the system toward self-consistency. Because L is
an expectation over ρθ, it concentrates on regions where
the physical density has support: the score need not be
accurate where no particles sample.
Theorem—Suppose the score sθ achieves (a) L[sθ] =
0 and (b) induces a Bohmian flow whose density remains
strictly positive on [0, T]. Then sθ(x, t) = ∇ln |Ψ(x, t)|2,
where Ψ is the unique solution of the TDSE (1) evolving
from the prescribed initial wave function; in particular,
the wave function (and hence its density and phase) is
fully recovered. The proof is detailed in the End Matter.

Bohmian trajectories. The score network sθ determines the

The loss (6) depends on θ through the score sθ, the flow
Jacobian F, and the sampling distribution ρθ. Since ini-
tial positions xi(0) ∼ρ0 are fixed, gradients flow end-
to-end through the trajectory ordinary differential equa-
tion (ODE) via the chain rule. The full gradient dL/dθ
is computed by backpropagation through time (BPTT)
along the discretized leapfrog trajectory, with gradient
checkpointing [19] to manage memory.
The algorithm
chains 5 spatial-derivative orders of φθ, plus the parame-
ter gradient via BPTT. The full derivative ladder is given
in the End Matter, Table I. Gradient stability is aided by
the symplecticity of the leapfrog integrator, which con-
strains the growth of Jacobian products. Figure 2 sum-
marizes the resulting computational loop.

The score is decom-

and classical trajectory focusing appears transiently. We

Discussion—
Bohm’s theory was famously regarded
as a conceptual framework to interpret quantum mechan-
ics [8, 9].

trajectories turns it into a practical computational tool
for the TDSE, leveraging machinery from modern gen-
erative modeling. The link between score matching and
quantum mechanics in fact predates that machinery it-
self. Already in 2003, Garashchuk and Rassolov [15, 16]
fitted the quantum potential on trajectories by minimiz-
ing Eρ[ 1
2|s|2 + ∇·s] ∝⟨Q⟩in a polynomial basis — the
implicit score-matching loss of Hyv¨arinen [17] up to con-
stants. What modern generative modeling contributes—
which we leverage here—is a flexible neural parametriza-
tion of the score, automatic differentiation through long
trajectories, and a globally enforced self-consistent objec-
tive over the entire time horizon, rather than an instan-
taneous least-squares fit at each timestep.
The parallel between generative modeling and quan-
tum mechanics extends from deterministic trajectories
to stochastic ones. Nelson’s stochastic mechanics [21, 22]
is a Schr¨odinger-equivalent formulation in which par-
ticles follow a drift–diffusion process rather than the
deterministic Bohmian path;
the drift combines the
Bohmian velocity with an osmotic term proportional to
the score, v + (ℏ/2m)∇ln ρ. In modern generative mod-
eling, flow-based models transport densities along de-
terministic ODEs, while diffusion-based models [12, 13]
use stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with a score-
proportional drift, the two linked by a probability-
flow ODE that reproduces the SDE’s marginals.
The
Bohmian ODE is precisely the probability-flow ODE of
Nelson’s SDE: Bohmian mechanics is to flow-based gen-
erative models what Nelson’s stochastic mechanics is to
diffusion-based ones. The same viewpoint underlies re-
cent neural methods for the Fokker–Planck equation [23–
27], which replace SDE simulation by integration of a
deterministic ODE driven by a self-consistently learned
score or velocity field. We extend this construction to
Schr¨odinger dynamics. The broader toolkit of modern
generative modeling, including denoising score match-


5
ing and flow matching [28–30], may extend naturally
to quantum dynamics. Orlova et al. [31] have taken a
first step on the stochastic side with Deep Stochastic
Mechanics: they parametrize both the current and os-
motic velocities of Nelson’s process as neural networks,
sample trajectories self-consistently by Euler–Maruyama
integration of the learned SDE, and train the networks by
minimizing partial differential equation (PDE) residuals
of the corresponding velocity equations on those sam-
ples.
The sampling strategy is thus self-generated as
in the present method, but the governing dynamics are
stochastic rather than deterministic, two velocity fields
are learned instead of a single score, and the loss is a
PDE residual rather than the Fisher divergence.
Other neural approaches to the TDSE differ more
sharply.
Time-dependent
variational
Monte
Carlo
(tVMC) [2, 32], among the most established neural-
variational methods for quantum dynamics, parametrizes
the complex wave function and evolves its parameters
in time by projecting the TDSE onto the tangent space
of the parameter manifold via the time-dependent vari-
ational principle [33, 34].
This projection requires in-
verting an often ill-conditioned quantum geometric ten-
sor at every integrator step, together with Monte Carlo
sampling from the time-dependent wave function. The
present method trades nodal flexibility for a real-valued,
density-only representation that is free of sign and phase,
replaces the instantaneous tangent-space projection by a
single global loss over the time horizon, replaces Metropo-
lis sampling of particle coordinates at every step by
a deterministic particle ensemble transported along the
Bohmian trajectories, and needs no metric inversion at
all.
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [35] are an-
other widely used neural framework for solving PDEs
that has been applied to the TDSE. PINNs parametrize
the complex space–time wave function Ψθ(x, t) directly
and minimize the TDSE residual on a set of colloca-
tion points drawn from a user-prescribed distribution
over configuration space and time.
As in the present
method, the optimization is a single global loss over the
time horizon, but the collocation distribution is chosen
by hand rather than by the dynamics: equal weight is
given to regions the physical state never visits, and ac-
curacy degrades in the tails where |Ψ|2 is small. A re-
cent application of PINNs to the fermionic TDSE [36]
samples collocation from |Ψθ|2 at each fixed t to bring
the training distribution onto the physical support. A
related global-in-time scheme [37] expands the complex
wave function in a fixed neural-quantum-state basis with
time-dependent coefficients, and likewise samples from
|Ψθ|2 at each time-integration node. The present method
drops the complex phase via the Madelung passage and
replaces user-prescribed collocation or |Ψθ|2 sampling by
a self-generated particle ensemble transported along the
Bohmian trajectories, automatically allocating the train-
ing effort where the density has support.
Closer
in
spirit
to
the
present
method
is
the
parametrized Wasserstein Hamiltonian flow (WHF) of
Ref. [38], which likewise eliminates the complex wave
function and casts Schr¨odinger dynamics as a continu-
ous normalizing flow on the probability density.
Like
tVMC, however, WHF projects the TDSE onto the pa-
rameter manifold at each instant and integrates the re-
sulting ODE for the neural-network parameters step by
step. The present method replaces this integrator-driven
projection by a global optimization of the Fisher diver-
gence over the time horizon, endowed with a built-in con-
vergence diagnostic (L = 0 iff self-consistent).
Fermionic wave functions generically have nodes: anti-
symmetry under particle exchange forces Ψ = 0 on a set
that partitions configuration space into sign-disconnected
cells [39]. These nodes violate the ρθ > 0 hypothesis of
the present analysis on two counts. First, at a node, the
score s = ∇ln ρ diverges and Bohmian trajectories can-
not cross. A smooth score network sθ = ∇φθ cannot
represent the resulting cell structure. Second, nodes res-
urrect the Wallstrom objection [40]: the Madelung sys-
tem recovers the Schr¨odinger equation only under the
quantization condition
H
v · dℓ= 2πnℏ/m, n ∈Z, on
every closed loop in configuration space, a constraint au-
tomatic for a single-valued Ψ but invisible to a score-
only formulation.
A possible route that resolves both
issues is to employ the fermion flow architecture [41–
43], which parametrizes many-electron wave functions
as a permutation-equivariant normalizing flow from a
Slater determinant. A diffeomorphism maps nodal cells
to nodal cells, so within each cell ρ > 0 and the phase-
free dynamics of Eq. (5) applies. The sign across cells
is read off the Slater determinant rather than learned
by the score network.
The Slater determinant is also
single-valued with integer phase winding fixed by its or-
bitals, and a diffeomorphism preserves that winding on
every closed loop, so the Wallstrom condition is auto-
matically satisfied. Combining such fermionic flow archi-
tectures with self-consistent score matching is a promis-
ing path toward real-time quantum dynamics of many-
electron systems.

Proof of the exactness theorem
We prove the Exactness Theorem by constructing the
wave function Ψ = √ρθ eiS/ℏexplicitly from sθ and ver-
ifying that it satisfies the TDSE (1). The construction
also provides the practical recipe for recovering the den-
sity and phase from a trained score.
(i) Self-consistency. The network sθ and the score
∇ln ρθ of the density ρθ that it induces through the flow
driven by Q[sθ] are, a priori, distinct fields. Since L ≥0
with equality iff its integrand vanishes on the support of
ρθ, hypothesis (a) forces sθ(x, t) = ∇ln ρθ(x, t) wherever
ρθ > 0, identifying Q[sθ] with the Madelung quantum
potential Q[∇ln ρθ].
(ii) Density. The Bohmian flow driven by sθ pushes ρ0
forward to ρθ(x(t), t) = ρ0(x(0))/|det F(t)| — the recipe
for the density. Probability is therefore exactly conserved
on Lagrangian particles, and the Madelung continuity
equation (2) holds by construction.
(iii) Existence of a phase. The initial velocity v(0) =
∇S(x, 0)/m is irrotational.
Expanding the material
derivative, the Bohmian equation m dv/dt = −∇(V +Q)
reads ∂tv = −∇(V + Q)/m −(v · ∇)v.
Taking the
curl and using the vorticity identity ∇× [(v · ∇)v] =
(v·∇)ω −(ω·∇)v + ω(∇·v) with ω ≡∇×v yields the
standard vorticity equation dω/dt = (ω·∇)v −ω(∇·v),
whose right-hand side is linear in ω. Hence ω(0) = 0
is preserved along trajectories. A single-valued phase S
with v = ∇S/m therefore exists for all t ∈[0, T].
(iv) Quantum Hamilton–Jacobi equation. Substituting

In d spatial dimensions, the per-step cost is O(d2) for
propagating the deformation gradient F and its veloc-
ity counterpart G via the variational equations.
The
score-transport term ∇x(0) ln |det F| can be evaluated by
d forward-mode tangent passes (O(d3) total) or a single
reverse-mode pass (O(d2)). This O(d2) overhead is fun-
damental to second-order dynamics. In first-order prob-
ability flows for the Fokker–Planck equation [23–27], the
score enters the velocity directly through the probability-
flow ODE, the velocity gradient ∂v/∂x is a local Jacobian
of a neural network, and the Hutchinson trace estima-
tor [10, 44] recovers O(d) scaling. In Bohmian dynamics,
the score enters one derivative deeper, through the ac-
celeration ¨x = −∇(V + Q(s)), so the velocity gradient
∂v/∂x = GF −1 is a trajectory-dependent quantity that
requires the full d × d deformation gradient.
